note: Hand-researched from each site's own agency findings (ATSDR / state health / EPA); see cites. Regenerate only by re-reading the sources.

sites.name: LOWER PASSAIC RIVER AND NEWARK BAY
sites.kind: EPA SUPERFUND SITE, LISTED 1984 · THE RIVER AND BAY BED
sites.gist: ROWING IS FINE · DON’T EAT ANY FISH OR CRAB
sites.what: Dioxin, PCBs and mercury in the bed of the lower Passaic River and Newark Bay, much of the dioxin from the old Diamond Alkali pesticide plant on Lister Avenue in Newark.
routes: On the tidal Passaic, up to Dundee Dam, no one should eat any fish or crab, and taking blue crab is banned. In Newark Bay and the Kills, blue crab is banned too; children, pregnant or nursing women and women who may become pregnant should eat none of the fish, and everyone else should keep striped bass, white perch and eel to four meals a year.
EPA’s risk study looked at boaters, and found the risk above its limits came from eating the catch, not from being on the water.
The state classes the lower river for boating and fishing, not swimming, and EPA calls the river not swimmable today. Some exposed mud on the east bank carried dioxin, an area the cleanup covers.
sites.act: Row or paddle if you like; don’t eat or keep anything you catch.
sites.src: EPA Record of Decision, 2021; New Jersey fish advisories

sites.name: PORTLAND HARBOR
sites.kind: EPA SUPERFUND SITE, LISTED 2000 · THE RIVER BED, CLEANUP UNDER WAY
sites.gist: SWIMMING AND MOST BEACHES ARE FINE · DON’T EAT BASS, CARP OR CATFISH
sites.what: PCBs, dioxins, oil compounds and pesticides in the bed of the lower Willamette River, from a century of shipyards, plants and docks along the harbor.
routes: Don’t eat bass, carp, brown bullhead (catfish) or clams, or most other fish that live in the river year round; crappie is the one, at up to two meals a month. Salmon, steelhead, shad and trout are the good choices.

The contamination is bound to the river bottom and in the resident fish; the state says the levels in the water are too low to harm health. As in any city river, swimming right after long, heavy rain is not advised.
Most harbor beaches pose little risk. The exceptions are the former GASCO beach and Willamette Cove, where no one should play on the beach or shoreline.
sites.act: Swim and paddle if you like; if you fish, keep salmon and steelhead and release the bass, carp and catfish.
sites.src: Oregon Health Authority public health assessment, 2011; Lower Willamette fish advisory, 2018

sites.name: LOWER DUWAMISH WATERWAY
sites.kind: EPA SUPERFUND SITE, LISTED 2001 · THE RIVER BED, CLEANUP UNDER WAY
sites.gist: BEACHES AND SWIMMING ARE FINE · EAT ONLY THE SALMON
sites.what: PCBs, arsenic, dioxins and oil compounds in the bed of the lower Duwamish River, from nearly a century of industry along its banks between Georgetown and South Park.
routes: No one should eat crab, clams, mussels or resident fish such as sole, flounder, perch and rockfish from the waterway. Salmon pass through quickly and are the healthy choice.

The state health department found that touching the mud while playing, fishing or net-fishing is not expected to harm health. Washing hands and face afterward, and children’s hands and toys, keeps it that way.
The chemicals in the water are not expected to harm swimmers. Stay out near sewer overflows for two days after heavy rain.
sites.act: Use the river and beaches; if you fish, keep only salmon.
sites.src: Washington State Department of Health assessment, 2003, and fish advisory

sites.name: LOWER FOX RIVER AND GREEN BAY
sites.kind: EPA SUPERFUND SITE, PROPOSED 1998 · THE RIVER BED, CLEANUP DONE 2020
sites.gist: SWIMMING AND BOATING ARE FINE · NO CARP, CATFISH OR MUSKY
sites.what: PCBs in the bed of the lower Fox River and Green Bay, from paper mills that recycled carbonless copy paper in the 1950s and 1960s. The dredging and capping finished in 2020; the fish will take years longer to clear.
routes: Below the De Pere Dam, no one should eat carp, channel catfish, bigmouth buffalo or musky, and white bass and large northern pike are a half meal a month. Walleye, perch, crappie and most others are one meal a month, or four for yellow perch and rock bass. In Green Bay, skip carp, musky and lake sturgeon. The advice is the same for everyone.
The state health assessment found that contact with the river mud and water while swimming, wading or boating is not expected to harm health.
The same assessment looked at drinking river water and found it was not a meaningful source of PCBs; eating the fish is the route that matters.
sites.act: Swim and boat if you like; if you fish, check Wisconsin’s Choose Wisely table for the stretch you fish before you keep anything.
sites.src: Wisconsin health department and ATSDR assessment, 2006; Choose Wisely fish advice, 2026

sites.name: KALAMAZOO RIVER
sites.kind: EPA SUPERFUND SITE, LISTED 1990 · THE RIVER, CREEK AND FLOODPLAIN, CLEANUP UNDER WAY
sites.gist: SWIMMING AND WADING ARE FINE · DON’T EAT THE FISH
sites.what: PCBs from paper mills that de-inked recycled paper, in Portage Creek and the Kalamazoo River from Kalamazoo to Lake Michigan, in the river bed, its banks and its floodplain.
routes: From Morrow Dam to Allegan Dam, including Lake Allegan, no one should eat any fish. Below Allegan Dam, most species are do-not-eat; walleye, yellow perch, rock bass and suckers are “Limited”: none for children under 15, anyone pregnant, nursing or planning children, and once or twice a year for everyone else.
The state health department found that touching or swallowing river water and mud while swimming or wading is not an important source of PCBs.
Backyards EPA sampled along the river near Otsego had PCBs well below the health-based level. Bare floodplain soil in the old dam ponds runs higher, and EPA’s cleanup digs it out.
sites.act: Swim and paddle if you like; release what you catch.
sites.src: EPA Record of Decision, 2022; Michigan Eat Safe Fish Guide, 2026

sites.name: HOUSATONIC RIVER
sites.kind: EPA SUPERFUND SITE, PROPOSED 1997 · THE RIVER AND ITS FLOODPLAIN
sites.gist: THE WATER AND AIR ARE FINE · DON’T EAT THE CATCH
sites.what: PCBs from General Electric’s Pittsfield plant, released from the 1930s to the 1970s, in the river mud, the floodplain soil and the wildlife, from Pittsfield down into Connecticut.
routes: Massachusetts advises that no one eat them from the river or its tributaries, from Dalton to the Connecticut line. In Connecticut, follow that state’s own fish advice.
No one should eat mallards or wood ducks from the river between Pittsfield and Rising Pond in Great Barrington.
EPA found the PCB risk from the river water and the air below its level of concern. Fishing is fine if you release what you catch.
Touching some floodplain soil and riverbank mud, and eating food grown in the floodplain, are risks EPA found along the river below Pittsfield, where the cleanup is now under way.
The contaminated areas around the Pittsfield plant and the first two miles of river are cleaned up; the rest of the river is being cleaned under EPA’s 2020 permit.
sites.act: Fish and paddle if you like, but release the catch and don’t eat ducks from the river.
sites.src: Massachusetts Department of Public Health advisory; EPA risk assessment, 2005

sites.name: ANNISTON PCB SITE
sites.kind: EPA SUPERFUND ALTERNATIVE SITE, NOT LISTED · YARDS AND CREEKS AROUND THE OLD MONSANTO PLANT
sites.gist: TAP WATER: NOT A ROUTE · DON’T EAT THE CREEK FISH
sites.what: PCBs from the former Monsanto plant, which made them from 1929 to 1971, in yard soil west of downtown and in Snow Creek, Choccolocco Creek and their floodplains.
routes: Homes and businesses here drink municipal water, not the groundwater under the site.

Yards were sampled, and where the top foot of soil was over EPA’s cleanup level it was dug out and replaced. Most have been cleaned; the rest are mostly overgrown wooded lots or yards whose owners declined.
Alabama advises eating no fish of any kind from Choccolocco Creek, and EPA says the same for Snow Creek. Eating fish is the main way PCBs reach people.
EPA chose the cleanup for Choccolocco Creek and its floodplain in December 2024; the Snow Creek work is being designed.
sites.act: Ask EPA whether your yard was sampled and cleaned, and don’t eat fish from Snow or Choccolocco Creek.
sites.src: EPA site profile and 2017 cleanup plan; Alabama fish advisory, 2026

sites.name: TAR CREEK
sites.kind: EPA SUPERFUND SITE, LISTED 1983 · OLD LEAD AND ZINC MINES OF OTTAWA COUNTY
sites.gist: YARD SOIL: THE ONE TO CHECK · KEEP CHILDREN OFF THE CHAT
sites.what: Lead, zinc and cadmium from a century of mining, left in piles of gravelly waste called chat, in yard soil and dust, and in creeks fed by mine water.
routes: Lead in yard soil was the main way children were exposed. Yards and public areas across the county have been cleaned and children’s blood lead has fallen sharply; any yard never sampled can still be tested for free.
Don’t use chat in a driveway, yard or garden, and don’t let children play on it.

Oklahoma sets monthly meal limits for some fish from the Spring and Neosho rivers, Grand Lake and the mill ponds, mostly bottom fish like carp, buffalo and sucker, with tighter limits for people who live in the area. Lead collects in bones, so boneless, skinless fillets are the safer choice.

The area’s water supply, the deep Roubidoux aquifer, is monitored every year, and old wells that could let mine water down into it keep being plugged. Shallow private wells found unsafe were closed and those homes put on city water.
The Ottawa County Health Department tests children from six months to six years for lead at no cost.
sites.act: If your yard in Ottawa County has never been sampled, ask Oklahoma DEQ for the free test.
sites.src: Oklahoma DEQ site page and fish advisory; EPA site profile

sites.name: BUNKER HILL · SILVER VALLEY
sites.kind: EPA SUPERFUND SITE, LISTED 1983 · THE SILVER VALLEY AND COEUR D’ALENE BASIN
sites.gist: CLEANED YARDS ARE CAPPED · LEAD REMAINS ON BEACHES AND RIVERBANKS
sites.what: Lead, arsenic and other metals from more than a century of mining and smelting, in soil, river sediment and the Coeur d’Alene River floodplain, from the Silver Valley down to Coeur d’Alene Lake.
routes: Yards and public spaces across the valley have had their topsoil removed and replaced, and children’s blood lead has dropped by more than half. Lead can still sit under that clean layer, in crawl spaces and in house dust.
Yard digging and some indoor projects need a permit from Panhandle Health District, at no cost, so the clean barrier stays intact.

Lead remains on many sandy beaches and banks along the Coeur d’Alene River and in its floodplain. Follow posted signs, wash hands before eating, eat on a table or blanket, and rinse off people and pets before heading home.
Don’t drink or wash with water from creeks or rivers here; bring your own.
Fish here were tested for lead, arsenic, cadmium and mercury. Idaho’s meal limits for the river, the chain lakes and Coeur d’Alene Lake are for mercury in some species.
Panhandle Health District tests anyone who lives, works or plays here, at no cost.
sites.act: Before digging or remodeling, get Panhandle Health District’s free permit; it can also tell you whether your yard was cleaned.
sites.src: Panhandle Health District and Idaho DEQ guidance; EPA site profile; Idaho fish advisory, 2020

sites.name: LIBBY ASBESTOS
sites.kind: EPA SUPERFUND SITE, LISTED 2002 · LIBBY, TROY AND THE OLD VERMICULITE MINE
sites.gist: TOWN CLEANUP FINISHED AND PROTECTIVE · CALL BEFORE YOU DIG OR REMODEL
sites.what: Asbestos from the old vermiculite mine near Libby, spread through insulation, soil and dust in Libby and Troy. Breathing the fibers can cause lung disease and cancer.
routes: EPA finished cleaning homes, businesses, schools and parks in Libby and Troy in 2018, and its 2025 review found that cleanup protective. Asbestos in the downtown air is far lower than when the mine ran.

Disturbing leftover vermiculite or old soil can release fibers. Before renovating or digging, call the Lincoln County Asbestos Resource Program; it has property records and can seek funding for sampling or removal.

The former mine and the forest around it are the one part not yet cleaned; EPA expects to propose a plan in 2027. In a wildfire there, protecting yourself from the smoke also protects you from the asbestos.
sites.act: Before you renovate or dig in Libby or Troy, call the Asbestos Resource Program; it can also tell you whether a property was tested and cleaned.
sites.src: EPA site profile and 2025 five-year review

sites.name: USS LEAD
sites.kind: EPA SUPERFUND SITE, LISTED 2009 · THE YARDS OF THE CALUMET NEIGHBORHOOD
sites.gist: TAP WATER: NOT A ROUTE · YARDS TESTED AND CLEANED
sites.what: Lead and arsenic from a century of smelting settled into yards here. EPA has tested the neighborhood’s yards and replaced the soil wherever it was high; the former housing complex is now an industrial lot.
routes: EPA sampled every yard and replaced contaminated soil with clean fill; that work is finished. EPA is now rechecking it against its stricter 2025 lead level.
Homes with high yard soil had their indoor dust tested, and cleaned at no cost where it was high. That work is finished too.
The water comes from Lake Michigan, not the groundwater under the site. Lead service pipes in older homes are a separate question, for the city’s water utility.
Before the cleanup, young children in the Calumet neighborhood and the housing complex had higher blood lead than elsewhere in the city. ATSDR urges testing for every child under 6.
sites.act: If you have a child under 6 here, ask your doctor or the East Chicago Health Department for a blood lead test.
sites.src: ATSDR health consultation, 2018; EPA site pages, 2026

sites.name: OMAHA LEAD
sites.kind: EPA SUPERFUND SITE, LISTED 2003 · YARDS AROUND DOWNTOWN OMAHA
sites.gist: TAP WATER: NOT A ROUTE · UNTESTED YARDS: THE ONE TO CHECK
sites.what: Lead from the smokestacks of a refinery and a battery recycler that ran for over a century settled on yards around downtown. EPA replaced the soil at most yards that needed it; the city is finishing the rest.
routes: Swallowed soil is the main way the lead reaches young children. Testing, and any cleanup, costs the owner nothing; the Omaha Lead Registry shows whether a property has been done.
The Douglas County Health Department tests indoor dust and provides HEPA vacuums to eligible homes.
A minor route, mostly from soil on the produce. The county advises washing and peeling, and raised beds for leafy and root crops where soil lead is high.
The water is tested at the plant and the tap, and the lead stays in the top few inches of soil, so ATSDR does not expect harmful lead in drinking water.
sites.act: If your yard isn’t marked done in the Omaha Lead Registry, ask the city for the free test, and have children under 7 tested for lead each year.
sites.src: ATSDR public health assessment, 2005; EPA site profile

sites.name: WESTSIDE LEAD
sites.kind: EPA SUPERFUND SITE, LISTED 2022 · YARDS IN ENGLISH AVENUE AND VINE CITY, CLEANUP UNDER WAY
sites.gist: YARD SOIL: THE ONE TO CHECK · EPA TESTS IT FREE
sites.what: Lead in yard soil, likely from foundry slag once used as fill in English Avenue and Vine City. EPA is testing yards and replacing the soil wherever lead is high.
routes: Children can swallow the soil while playing, and mowing or digging stirs it up. EPA tests yards and replaces contaminated soil at no cost to owners or tenants.
Soil tracked in on shoes and pets becomes house dust. The state health department advises wet-mopping hard floors and washing children’s hands after outdoor play.
The state health department advises raised beds or containers, and washing and peeling anything grown in the ground.
EPA encourages a lead blood test for young children; ask your family doctor or a local health center.
sites.act: If your yard hasn’t been tested, sign EPA’s access form for the free test; owners and tenants both qualify.
sites.src: EPA site profile and cleanup memo, 2022; Georgia Department of Public Health

sites.name: VASQUEZ BOULEVARD AND I-70
sites.kind: EPA SUPERFUND SITE, LISTED 1999 · YARDS IN NORTHEAST DENVER NEIGHBORHOODS
sites.gist: TAP WATER AND GARDENS: FINE · YARDS NEVER CLEANED: THE ONE TO CHECK
sites.what: Arsenic and lead from two old smelters, in yards in Cole, Clayton, Elyria-Swansea, Globeville and northern Curtis Park. EPA replaced the soil in the yards that needed it in the 2000s and is now rechecking against its stricter 2025 lead level.
routes: Most yards were tested and replaced where needed. Where an owner declined, EPA sends a yearly letter about the soil.
If your yard’s soil was never replaced, EPA recommends a lead blood test for young children every year.
ATSDR found the vegetables take up far too little to harm the people who eat them. EPA still suggests washing produce and peeling root crops.
Homes here drink mountain surface water, not the groundwater under the old smelters.
sites.act: If your yard was never replaced, have children under 7 tested for lead every year, as EPA advises.
sites.src: ATSDR public health assessment, 2003; EPA Record of Decision, 2003; EPA five-year review, 2024

sites.name: BUTTE AND SILVER BOW CREEK
sites.kind: EPA SUPERFUND SITE, LISTED 1983 · BUTTE, WALKERVILLE AND THE CREEK
sites.gist: YARDS AND ATTIC DUST: THE ONE TO CHECK · TESTING IS FREE
sites.what: Lead, arsenic and mercury from a century of mining, milling and smelting, in yards, house dust and attic dust across Butte and Walkerville. In 2026 EPA lowered its lead cleanup level and widened the area, so many more homes now qualify for testing and cleanup.
routes: Swallowed soil is the main way it reaches children. Butte-Silver Bow’s Residential Metals Abatement Program tests yards free for anyone in the Butte area and replaces the soil where needed.
Old smelter dust can sit in attics and sift into the rooms below; the same free program tests it and removes it. EPA advises shoes off at the door, damp-mopping and wiping sills.
If you’re unsure of your soil, EPA advises raised beds with lead-free soil, and washing and peeling what you grow.
Swimming and eating the fish are barred at the treatment ponds at the creek’s lower end.
sites.act: Call Butte-Silver Bow’s Residential Metals Abatement Program for a free test of your yard and dust.
sites.src: EPA Record of Decision Amendment, 2026; EPA site pages

sites.name: SAN JACINTO RIVER WASTE PITS
sites.kind: EPA SUPERFUND SITE, LISTED 2008 · OLD PAPER-MILL WASTE PITS IN THE RIVER
sites.gist: LIMIT OR SKIP THE FISH AND CRAB · TAP WATER: NOT A ROUTE
sites.what: Dioxins from paper-mill waste dumped in pits beside the river in the 1960s and 1970s. One pit has been dug out; the other is capped and set to be dug out.
routes: Women of childbearing age and children under 12 should eat none from the river below the Lake Houston Dam or the Houston Ship Channel; other adults, no more than one 8-ounce meal a month.
Touching or swallowing the waste-pit mud again and again, over a year or more, could harm health. The pits are fenced and roped off.
Not expected to add to health risk; the dioxins cling to the mud, not the water.
Not expected to add to health risk; the chemicals do not readily get into the air.
Channelview’s water comes from the county water district, not from the brackish groundwater by the pits.
sites.act: Follow the state’s fish advice: limit or skip fish and blue crab from this river and the Ship Channel.
sites.src: Texas DSHS fish advisory ADV-55 and DSHS/ATSDR assessment, 2012

sites.name: MONTROSE CHEMICAL
sites.kind: EPA SUPERFUND SITE, LISTED 1989 · UNDER THE GROUND HERE
sites.gist: TAP WATER: NOT A ROUTE · INDOOR AIR: TESTED, NO RISK FOUND
sites.what: A former DDT plant. DDT remains in soil at the old plant, and solvents (chlorobenzene, TCE and benzene) in the groundwater under the area, mixed with the plume from the neighboring Del Amo site.
routes: No one drinks or uses the contaminated groundwater. The area’s tap water is tested regularly and is safe to drink.
EPA studied whether vapors from the groundwater get into buildings and found no health risk in the neighborhoods near the site.
Where DDT reached home yards, on Kenwood Avenue and West 204th Street, EPA dug out the soil and restored the yards.
The DDT that went down the sewers to the ocean is a separate matter: see PALOS VERDES SHELF.
sites.act: Nothing to do at home; if you fish the coast, follow the Palos Verdes fish advice.
sites.src: EPA site updates, 2020 and 2024

sites.name: PALOS VERDES SHELF
sites.kind: EPA SUPERFUND SITE, LISTED 1989 · THE OCEAN FLOOR OFFSHORE
sites.gist: SWIMMING AND SURFING ARE FINE · DON’T EAT WHITE CROAKER
sites.what: DDT and PCBs from the old Montrose plant and other industries, sent out through the sewers from the 1940s to the 1980s, on the ocean floor off the Palos Verdes Peninsula. The floor is too deep to touch; the chemicals build up in some fish.
routes: From Santa Monica Pier to Seal Beach Pier, no one should eat white croaker (kingfish or tomcod), barred sand bass or topsmelt. Women 18 to 49 and children should also skip black croaker and Pacific barracuda.
The state lists how many servings a week of other species are fine. Eat only the skinless fillet; the chemicals collect in the skin, fat and guts.
sites.act: Don’t eat white croaker, barred sand bass or topsmelt caught along this coast.
sites.src: California OEHHA fish advisory and EPA fact sheet, 2023

sites.name: SAN GABRIEL VALLEY GROUNDWATER
sites.kind: EPA SUPERFUND SITE, LISTED 1984 · FOUR AREAS OF GROUNDWATER UNDER THE VALLEY
sites.gist: TAP WATER: TREATED TO MEET STANDARDS · INDOOR AIR: TESTED WHERE NEEDED
sites.what: Industrial solvents (TCE and PCE) and other chemicals, including perchlorate and NDMA, in the groundwater under parts of the valley, the same aquifer much of its drinking water comes from.
routes: Water from contaminated wells is treated before it is served. Water agencies must meet state and federal drinking water standards and test their wells regularly to show it.
Where the solvents sit close to the surface in El Monte and South El Monte, EPA tested homes and businesses; where vapor was getting in, it fitted systems or air purifiers and keeps checking them.
Pumping and treating the groundwater to stop it spreading; much of the cleaned water goes into the drinking supply.
sites.act: To see what is in your tap water, read your water provider’s yearly water quality report.
sites.src: EPA progress update, 2021, and five-year review, 2022

sites.name: WELLS G&H
sites.kind: EPA SUPERFUND SITE, LISTED 1983 · UNDER THE GROUND HERE
sites.gist: TAP WATER: NOT A ROUTE · INDOOR AIR: TESTED, NO RISK FOUND
sites.what: Solvents (TCE and PCE) and other industrial waste from nearby properties contaminated two city wells, found in 1979; the wells were shut. Cleanup of the groundwater and soil goes on.
routes: Wells G and H have been shut since 1979. The city supplies its water from other sources, and no private wells draw from this area.
EPA checks the air in the building next to the old UniFirst property every year and has found no risk to the people inside; new buildings on the old Grace property have systems that keep vapor out.
The contaminated soil is on the old industrial properties being cleaned up, and the Aberjona River’s sediment cleanup was finished in 2017.
sites.act: Nothing to do at home; Woburn’s tap water does not come from these wells.
sites.src: EPA five-year review, 2019

sites.name: LOVE CANAL
sites.kind: EPA SUPERFUND SITE, LISTED 1983, REMOVED 2004 · THE CAPPED LANDFILL
sites.gist: TAP WATER: NOT A ROUTE · HOME AIR TESTED, NO ISSUES FOUND
sites.what: Chemical waste buried in an unfinished canal in the 1940s and 1950s. It is sealed under a cap and fence, with a drain that collects and treats what leaks; the cleanup was finished in 1999.
routes: The neighborhood’s water comes from the City of Niagara Falls public supply; the groundwater here is not used for drinking.
Air sampling in homes in the surrounding area found no indoor air issues, and no homes sit close enough to the buried waste to need more testing.
Contaminated mud was cleaned out of the nearby sewers and of Black and Bergholtz creeks, and the creek beds were lined with clean stone.
Running the drain and treatment plant and checking the groundwater; EPA rates the cleanup protective. Some nearby land is limited to commercial or industrial use.
sites.act: Nothing to do; the landfill is fenced off and the cleanup is monitored.
sites.src: EPA five-year review, 2024
